map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks run left to right in process order. A card opens with a title band — the block's number badge, its name and its status — and carries a column of input ports on the left and output ports on the right; a port names the transition and the block at the other end, and a click on it takes the camera there. A transition that sends the work back is a dashed return port marked ↻, and every transition a block makes to itself shares the double port under the card. Long links travel through the nearest free lane between rows instead of over the whole diagram. The card also carries the run's state: how many times the block ran, how long its passes took and, when it works through a list, how far that list has got — hover a fact chip, a port or a line to light it and read the rest. The contents on the left jumps to any block and its finder answers "which block is this step in"; the toolbar's layout presets re-lay the diagram and return the camera to the block you were reading.

graph.title: Graph: every step of the definition
graph.body: The same run, step by step: each block is a tinted group and each step inside it a card with the same title band, ports and fact chips as on the map. The chips carry the step's directive, the fields it must return and its expressions — hover one to read the full text in a tooltip. An output port is named by the case that selects it, `success` and `default` are the outputs taken when no case holds, and `error` and `timeout` are control outputs; return ports and the double port under a card mark the loops. The step the run is on breathes, the steps it has been through are toned as done. The contents on the left moves the camera to a block's group, the finder in the toolbar jumps to a step and opens its panel, and the layout presets re-lay the groups — stacked, compact, in a row, or with the steps turned top to bottom.

map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks run left to right in process order. A card opens with a title band — the block's number badge and its name — and carries a column of input ports on the left and output ports on the right; a port names the transition and the block at the other end, and a click on it takes the camera there. A transition that sends the work back is a dashed return port marked ↻, and every transition a block makes to itself shares the double port under the card; hover a port or a line to light it and read the condition, the cause and the exit of a loop. Long links travel through the nearest free lane between rows instead of over the whole diagram. The contents on the left jumps to any block and its finder answers "which block is this step in"; the toolbar's layout presets re-lay the diagram, and the panel on the right holds the block's description, its steps and, in edit mode, the authoring controls.

graph.title: Graph: every step of the definition
graph.body: The definition step by step: each block is a tinted group and each step inside it a card with the same title band, ports and fact chips as on the map. The chips carry the step's directive, the fields it must return and its expressions — hover one to read the full text in a tooltip. An output port is named by the case that selects it, `success` and `default` are the outputs taken when no case holds, and `error` and `timeout` are control outputs; return ports and the double port under a card mark the loops. Clicking a card opens the node level of the right panel, where the directive, the completion condition, the returned fields, the cases, the connections, the validation and a catalog-drawn node's configuration are read in full. The contents on the left moves the camera to a block's group, the finder in the toolbar jumps to a step, and the layout presets re-lay the groups — stacked, compact, in a row, or with the steps turned top to bottom.

edit.hint: Edit mode changes the workflow definition itself — block names and descriptions, transition labels and loop explanations, which block a step belongs to, a step's directive or expressions, and the variable registry. It never touches a run. Edits live on the page until you save them, and Undo takes back the last one. Every change is checked at once: the process rules in the browser, then the whole definition on the server. Save opens only when both checks pass for exactly what you see, and it is refused if someone else changed the workflow in the meantime.
edit.guideTitle: You are editing the process definition
edit.guideBody: Change a block's name or description in place; click the pencil next to a transition to change its label or its loop's cause and exit; in the block panel, move a step to another block or edit its text; in Variables, edit the registry. Both views re-derive at once, rule violations appear as diagnostics, "Export" lists exactly which flow-file entries would change, and "Save" sends the definition to the server against the revision you loaded.

intro.title: Your agent does the work
intro.body: Moira is used through your AI agent: you describe a task, the agent runs a flow, and Moira gives it one step at a time and checks each result. This page shows where that work stands.

how.title: How it works
how.body: Three steps from zero to a checked result. When you know them, hide this panel; Settings → Preferences brings it back.

connect.title: Connect your agent
connect.body: Add Moira to your AI client once. Pick your client here and follow its few steps; the rest happens in the chat with your agent.

try.title: A first prompt to try
try.body: Say this to your agent on any small task. It runs Example 1: Simple Steps, and you can watch every step here.

practice.title: Practice by hand
practice.body: “Build your first flow” is a tutorial in the flow editor: on your own copy of Example 1 you add a step, connect it, add a choice and use a value from an earlier step, and each lesson is checked. It is optional — your agent builds real flows.

intro.title: Flows are made by your agent
intro.body: A flow is a process your agent follows step by step. You do not build one on this page: describe the task to your agent, and it runs a ready flow or creates a new one with the Workflow Management Flow, at a level you agree on — Simple, Standard or Complex. A flow built at the Simple level can later be taken through the fuller path: ask your agent again.

recommended.title: Recommended flows
recommended.body: Where to start: example flows that teach the basics, and ready flows for everyday tasks. Hide the panel once you know them; Settings → Preferences brings it back.

all.title: Every flow you can use

scopes.title: Whose flows

filters.title: Search and filters

level.title: The flow's level
level.body: A flow built with the Workflow Management Flow shows the level it was built at: Simple, Standard or Complex — how thoroughly it was designed and reviewed. The level is apart from the flow's subject tags.

practice.title: Practice by hand
practice.body: “Build your first flow” is a tutorial in the flow editor: on your own copy of Example 1 you add a step, connect it, add a choice and use a value from an earlier step, and each lesson is checked. It is optional — your agent builds real flows.

intro.title: Every run of a flow
intro.body: Each execution listed here is a run: one pass of a flow on one task. Your agent starts it, and Moira records every step it takes.

status.title: Filter by status

list.title: Open a run

intro.title: Notes your agents keep
intro.body: A note is a piece of text stored under a key, with tags to group it. Agents write and read notes as they work, so what one run learns the next one can use; you can read and edit them here.

create.title: Write a note yourself
create.body: Create a note with a unique key, tags and content. An agent finds it by that key.

list.title: Your notes and their history

intro.title: Reusable instructions
intro.body: A playbook is a piece of behaviour text written once and used by many flows: a flow's step refers to it by name, and the run reads its current text at every step.

create.title: Write a playbook

list.title: Your playbooks and their history

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. The contents on the left lists them in order, and the highlighted row is one block: a status icon, a coloured number badge, the name, and how far the block has got. The same badge and name head that block's card on the diagram, in its title band.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is the step the agent is on right now, in the Steps section of the block panel — click it and the panel opens the node level for that step, with a breadcrumb back to the block and its directive, completion condition, cases and connections in full.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back; the Returns section of the node level names each field with its type and whether it is required. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlight is a return port — the dashed pill marked ↻ on the card the work leaves from. It names the transition and where it goes; hover it to light the return line and read what causes the loop and what ends it, and click it to travel to the other end.

route.title: Every run leaves a route
route.body: A run is one execution of the process. Moira records its route: every step in order, every loop it went through, and the values the steps produced along the way. The highlight is this run's route cursor, in the toolbar of whichever view is open: drag it and the whole page — cards, panel and variables — goes back to that visit. The variables tab shows the values as they stood there, and any adjustment a person made is marked.

explore.title: Explore the same run your way
explore.body: The highlighted toolbar holds everything that changes what you see. The Map / Graph switch picks the view: the Map is the process with the run's state on it, the Graph is every step of the definition. The layout presets beside it re-lay both diagrams — rows, compact, balanced branches, top to bottom — and bring the camera back to the block you were reading. The magnifier finds a step by id or text, and the compass opens the note about the view that is open. Your selection and the camera survive a switch.

modes.title: Map and graph
modes.body: Map shows the run's stages as blocks, lit by where the run is and what it has done. Graph shows every node with the run's status on it, the technical picture. Both show the same run.

panel-tabs.title: The panel's tabs
panel-tabs.body: Block: the selected block and its steps. Variables: every value with its history — and the place to answer the waiting step yourself. Errors: what the run recorded going wrong. Steps: every step it took, in order. Locks: locks placed on this run.

answer.title: Answer the waiting step yourself
answer.body: The run waits at a step for an answer. You can give it here instead of the agent: fill in what the step asks for and send it. Moira checks it as it would the agent's answer, records it in the route as your adjustment, and the run goes on.

notifications.title: Where notifications lead
notifications.body: When this run needs you or moves on — a plan ready for approval, a result ready for review, the work finished — Moira can notify you. Each notification opens with the flow and the task, and its heading links to this page.

intro.title: You don't have to build flows
intro.body: Moira is made for agents. Describe your task to your agent in plain words: it picks a ready flow or creates one for you through the Workflow Management Flow — simple or complex, whatever fits. This page is for looking inside a flow when you are curious; nothing here is required.

steps.title: Read it as plain steps
steps.body: The Steps view shows the flow as what the agent is told: numbered instructions joined by arrows. Where the agent's answer decides the way on, the arrows fork and name the answer. With “Variables as words” on, every variable reads as ordinary words, so the whole flow reads like a list of instructions.

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. The contents on the left lists them in order, and the highlighted row is one block: a coloured number badge, the name and how long the block usually takes. The same badge and name head that block's card on the diagram, in its title band.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is one step of this block, in the Steps section of the block panel — click it and the page goes to that step on the graph and opens the node level of the panel, with its directive, completion condition, cases, connections and validation in full.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back; the Returns section of the node level names each field with its type and whether it is required. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlight is a return port — the dashed pill marked ↻ on the card the work leaves from. It names the transition and where it goes; hover it to light the return line and read what causes the loop and what ends it, and click it to travel to the other end.

edit.title: You can edit this flow here
edit.body: You own this flow, so the highlighted switch turns on edit mode: change block names and descriptions, transition labels, which block a step belongs to, a step's text and the variable registry. Both views update at once, and the server checks the definition when you save. Runs of this workflow are read on the run page.

edit-reader.title: Only its owner edits it
edit-reader.body: This page shows the definition, not a run: the header names the flow, its version, its description and its facts, and carries the page's actions. Only the flow's owner can edit it. To make your own version, use it as a template: you get a private copy you can change. Runs of this workflow are read on the run page.

explore.title: Explore the same process your way
explore.body: The highlighted toolbar holds everything that changes what you see. The Steps / Map / Graph switch picks the view: Steps is what the agent is told, the Map is the process the workflow declares, the Graph is every step of the definition. On the Map and the Graph, the layout presets re-lay the diagram — rows, compact, balanced branches, top to bottom — and bring the camera back to the block you were reading, the magnifier finds a step by id or text, and the compass opens the note about the view that is open. On Steps, the switch beside the view tabs reads variables as plain words. Your selection and the camera survive a switch.

facts.title: What the flow is about
facts.body: Under the name: what the flow is for, its subject tags and how many nodes it has. A flow's author writes the description and tags; they are how you tell flows apart in the list.

level.title: The level it was built at
level.body: A flow built with the Workflow Management Flow shows its level: Simple, Standard or Complex. You don't pick it on this page — when you ask your agent for a flow, it agrees the level with you. A Simple flow can later be taken through the fuller path by asking again.

modes.title: Three ways to look at it
modes.body: Steps reads the flow as numbered instructions. Map shows its stages as blocks with the paths between them. Graph shows every node and connection, the technical picture. They are one flow; switch whenever you like.

diagram-note.title: How to read this diagram
diagram-note.body: Each diagram has its own short note here: what the cards, colours and arrows of this view mean. Open it whenever a picture is unclear.

panel-tabs.title: The panel beside the diagram
panel-tabs.body: Block shows the selected block — what it does, where it leads, its steps — or, when a node is selected, that node in full. Variables lists the values the flow declares, each with its type, default and description.

playbook.title: A playbook the step reads
playbook.body: This node names a playbook: shared behaviour text the step includes when it runs. Its link opens the playbook's page; one that belongs to another account opens read-only.

template.title: Get a copy you can change
template.body: This flow is public. “Use as Template” makes your own private copy, which you can edit, rename and share. Or ask your agent to make a new flow for your task.

visibility.title: Who can see it
visibility.body: Private flows are yours alone; public ones appear in everyone's catalog and can be copied. Share creates invitation links that give chosen people access without making the flow public, and lists who has it.

nav.title: Jump between sections
nav.body: Every setting lives in one of these sections. Pick one to go straight to it; the section you are reading is marked as you scroll.

account.title: Your account
account.body: Your display name, email and username. The username is part of every workflow link you share, so change it with care.

security.title: Security & sign-in
security.body: Change your password and see every browser or device signed in to your account. Sign out any you do not recognise.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.body: Moira tells you when a run needs you or moves on: a plan ready for approval, a result ready for review, the work finished. Each notification opens with the flow and the task, and its heading links to the run's page. Set up here where they reach you, such as a Telegram bot, and send a test message to be sure it works.

github.title: GitHub & Codespaces
github.body: Connect GitHub and choose repositories so agents can work in cloud codespaces. Limits and automatic pausing are set here too.

apps.title: Connected apps
apps.body: AI assistants you have allowed to use Moira. Revoke any you no longer use.

tokens.title: API tokens
tokens.body: Keys for clients that cannot use the browser sign-in. A token is shown only once, when you create it.

preferences.title: Preferences
preferences.body: Choose the theme and language of the website. These apply in this browser.

steps.title: Three steps to connect
steps.body: Connect your GitHub account, install the Moira GitHub App, and grant it the repositories agents may work in. The current step is highlighted.

connect.title: Connect and install
connect.body: Connect your GitHub account and install the Moira App on your account or an organization. Choose its repositories on GitHub. When already connected, use Add account or organization, then Refresh here to see the new repositories.

codespaces.title: Create a codespace
codespaces.body: Pick a repository and branch, then create a personally billed codespace. Agents find it by ID. Stop keeps its files; Delete removes them. Refresh checks GitHub for changes made outside Moira.

limits.title: Know your limits
limits.body: GitHub's monthly personal compute, storage and billed amount appear above Moira's own limits when the App has Plan: read access. Stopped codespaces still use Moira's held slots.

autopause.title: Pause idle codespaces
autopause.body: Moira stops a codespace no agent has used through Moira for the time you choose, so it does not keep running up your GitHub bill. The next command starts it again.

bot.title: Create a bot
bot.body: In Telegram, message @BotFather, send /newbot and follow the prompts. Paste the token it gives you here and save.

chat.title: Find your chat ID
chat.body: Message @userinfobot in Telegram: the user ID it replies with is your chat ID. Paste it here and save, then send your own bot any message so it can write to you. Do not put the bot token into a browser URL.

enable.title: Turn it on
enable.body: Tick Send notifications to Telegram and save. The channel shows Ready when everything is in place.

test.title: Send a test
test.body: Send a test message. If it does not arrive, check the token and chat ID; the error message says which part failed.

firstRun.title: New to Moira?
firstRun.body: A short tour shows what each screen is for, on the screen itself. You can open it any time from “Show me around” in the sidebar.

try.title: Your first run
try.body: A run appears here when your agent runs a flow. To start one, say to your agent: “Use Moira to run Example 1: Simple Steps for this task: …”. Then open the run to watch it step by step.

bar.title: Your edits, before they are saved
bar.body: Every change collects here, not in the saved flow: the count, what exactly changes (the export), Undo for the last change and Reset for all of them. Nothing reaches the flow until you save.

add-step.title: Add a step
add-step.body: Adds a step to this block: pick its type and fill in what it requires. On the graph, right-click a connection to insert a step on it, or a step to add one after it.

step-actions.title: Rename or delete a step
step-actions.body: Renaming updates every reference to the step's id. Deleting asks where each connection that led to it should go instead.

blocks.title: Blocks
blocks.body: Blocks are the stages of the process. Add one here; the bin on a block's row in the contents deletes it once no step is left in it.

connections.title: Where a step leads
connections.body: Point each output at another step, add an output or remove one. A connection that crosses into another block needs a label saying why; you give it on the transition under “Where it leads”.

choice.title: Add a choice
choice.body: Makes the step end with a question and options: the agent answers with one option, and the answer picks the route. One option continues as before; each other leads to its own step, existing or new.

validation.title: What stops a save
validation.body: Moira checks the draft as you edit. Problems show next to the step or block they concern, and Save stays off until none blocks it.

stale.title: Saved against this revision
stale.body: A save is made against the revision you loaded. If the flow was saved elsewhere in the meantime, the save is refused rather than overwriting it: reload, and apply your change again.

editorOffer.title: New to editing?
editorOffer.body: A short tour shows where edits collect, how steps, blocks, connections and choices are changed, and what stops a save.

lesson-0.title: How flows are made
lesson-0.body: For real work you don't build flows by hand: you describe the task to your agent, and it builds the flow through the Workflow Management Flow, agreeing the depth with you — simple, standard or complex. This tutorial builds a small one by hand, so you can read and adjust what the agent makes.

lesson-1.title: Your own copy
lesson-1.body: You practise on your own private copy of the learning example, so nothing shared changes. Press “Use as Template” — or “Do it for me”.

lesson-2.title: Add a step
lesson-2.body: Add a step to the Do block with “Add step”, for example “Save a draft”, with a directive (what the agent does) and a completion condition (when it is done). A step must lead somewhere to be saved: in its connections point its success at check-result, and label that connection — it goes into the Check block, and every connection into another block says why. Save. Nothing leads to your step yet; the check says so, and that is the next lesson.

lesson-3.title: Connect it
lesson-3.body: Now lead the work through your step: point do-task's success at your new step, in do-task's connections. Every step is then on the way from start to the end. Save.

lesson-4.title: Add a choice
lesson-4.body: Make check-result end with a question: open it in the Check block and use “Add a choice”. Ask “Does the result match?” with the options yes and no. Yes continues to the report as before; no leads to a new step, “Explain what is missing”, in the Check block. The new step must lead on too: point it at end and label that connection, since it leaves the Check block. Save. This is the shape of Example 2, “One choice”.

lesson-5.title: Use a value from an earlier step
lesson-5.body: A step can use what an earlier step returned. In the report's directive, add {{ref}} — the task as the agent restated it at the start. Moira fills it in when the report step runs. Save.

lesson-6.title: Try it (optional)
lesson-6.body: The web app does not start runs; your agent does. Say this to your agent, and once the run is complete, check again here. Or skip this lesson.

lesson-7.title: What next
lesson-7.body: You have practised what your agent builds for you: steps, the connections between them, a choice decided by an answer, and a value carried from an earlier step. For real work you don't build flows by hand — ask your agent for a flow, and it builds it through the Workflow Management Flow, agreeing the depth with you. Your copy is no longer needed: you can delete it.

findings.copy-not-owned: This flow is not yours. Make your own copy with “Use as Template”.
findings.copy-not-private: Your copy should be private while you practise.
findings.copy-no-process: This copy has no process view, so it cannot be edited here.
findings.copy-structure-differs: This copy is not the unchanged example. Start from a fresh copy of the example.
findings.example-step-missing: The example's step “{{node}}” is gone. Put it back (Undo, or Discard edits).
findings.new-step-missing: There is no new step yet. Add one to the Do block with “Add step”.
findings.new-step-extra: There are {{count}} new steps; this lesson needs exactly one.
findings.new-step-directive-empty: The new step “{{node}}” has no directive: say what the agent does.
findings.new-step-condition-empty: The new step “{{node}}” has no completion condition: say when it is done.
findings.new-step-no-block: The new step “{{node}}” is in no block. Put it in the Do block.
findings.new-step-not-connected: “do-task” does not lead to your new step yet: point its success at “{{step}}”.
findings.new-step-not-continuing: Your new step “{{node}}” should lead on to “check-result”.
findings.dangling-connection: A connection of “{{node}}” leads to a step that does not exist.
findings.unreachable-node: No route reaches “{{node}}”: connect a step to it.
findings.route-without-end: From “{{node}}” no route reaches the end.
findings.edge-needs-label: The connection from “{{node}}” goes into another block and needs a label saying why.
findings.process-issue: The process reports a problem on “{{node}}” ({{issue}}).
findings.choice-field-missing: check-result does not ask a question yet: use “Add a choice” on it.
findings.case-not-reading-answer: A route of check-result does not compare its answer.
findings.case-compares-value-not-offered: A route compares “{{value}}”, which the answer does not offer.
findings.case-output-same-route: The option “{{field}}” leads where the default route goes; give it its own step.
findings.choice-loops-back: The option “{{field}}” comes back to check-result; lead it on towards the end.
findings.reference-missing: No step uses a value from an earlier step yet: add {{ref}} to the report.
findings.reference-field-not-declared: “{{reference}}” names a field that step does not return.
findings.reference-not-before-use: “{{reference}}” is used before its step has run.
findings.validation-errors: The flow still has {{count}} error(s) to fix before it can be saved.

tutorial.narrow: The tutorial edits the flow, and editing needs a larger screen. Open Moira on a computer: your progress is kept and waits for you there.
tutorial.haveCopy: You already have a copy from before: “Do it for me” opens it.
tutorial.notYourCopy: This is not your tutorial copy. Open the tutorial from “Show me around” to get back to it.
tutorial.conflict: The save was refused: your copy was changed elsewhere since this page loaded it. Reload to see the saved copy, then make your change again.
tutorial.broken: “{{lesson}}” no longer holds after your changes. Go back and fix it before going on.
